open-question.question: Once the sweep writes lift, fold, remove, and commit into its own batched call, does it still follow the two shared answer procedures for anything (the lift step's no-recommendation guard, the answer core's analyse questions), or does its own file state every per-question step and the two procedures say they are followed by the single-question skills alone, as the recommendation pass's batching did in its own file?
open-question.alternative: The sweep's own file states every per-question mechanical step its batched call runs: lift with its silent skip, the fold through the fold command, remove with the lifted option, and the commit. It stops following answer-with-recommendation-procedure.md altogether and keeps a reference to answer-procedure.md only for the judgment that call cannot do: the analyse step's questions, in whatever form the sweep keeps them, and the fold step's rules on what the decision text says (clean prose, no citation marker, the live document's section names). The lift procedure's intro names only answer-open-question-with-recommendation. The core's intro is reworded to say the sweep follows its analyse step and fold-content rules, not its tool steps. The CLAUDE.md sweep invariant and the shell-literal clause are reworded to match. The split is the recommendation pass's own: that pass still follows the shared pick procedure for its judgment and keeps every write, lift, and commit in its own fixed call. The sweep likewise keeps one home for the decision-writing rules it shares with every answer path, while its file is the only place its mechanics are described. The core's intro has to state a partial-follower relationship, which a later editor must keep accurate step by step. How much of the analyse step is left to reference depends on the mooting-cascade and contradiction-advisory questions; if both drop that judgment, the reference shrinks to the fold-content rules alone.

The sweep keeps following answer-with-recommendation-procedure.md and answer-procedure.md once per question, and both procedures' text stays as it is, their "followed ... once per question, by the inline answer sweep" sentences included. The sweep's own file lists where its batched call departs from them: no per-question locate (the compact view stands in for it), the fold written through the fold command instead of a file edit, the lift guard's stop turned into the silent skip it already is, and lift, fold, remove, and commit run inside the one call instead of as separate steps. The CLAUDE.md sweep invariant keeps "following answer-with-recommendation-procedure.md from its lift step", and the shell-literal clause still covers "the per-question calls of the procedures it follows". Smallest change. The shared procedures, the single-question skills that follow them, and the invariants that cite them stay untouched, and the analyse questions and fold-content rules (clean prose, no citation marker, the live document's section names) keep one home. The sweep would "follow" procedures whose locate, fold mechanism, guard behaviour, and step order it overrides almost entirely. A runner reading them could then run a locate or an Edit fold that the batched call never makes, which is the drift the batch exists to remove, and a later edit to the procedures has to be checked against a list of exceptions held in a different file.

The sweep keeps following both procedures, and the procedures themselves are edited to describe the sweep's batched form beside the single-question form. The answer core's locate step gets an exception for a caller holding the compact view, its fold step names the fold command for the sweep while the single-question skills keep their Edit-based fold, and the lift procedure's guard states the sweep's silent skip. The sweep's file shows the call and points at the procedures for what each section does, and the CLAUDE.md invariants keep naming the procedures as the sweep's. Each per-question rule still lives in exactly one file. Someone reading the answer procedures sees every path that records an answer, the batched one included, and the fold-before-remove and option-passing rules cannot drift between the sweep and the single-question skills. It adds the branches CLAUDE.md rules out: the recording core is meant to stay "a pass-through recorder that gained one input and no branch", and its inputs-as-given contract is shared with the literal answer-open-question. Every single-question runner would also read sweep-only text it must ignore, and the procedures would describe a shell call whose full form lives only in the sweep's file.

As with "Core judgment only", the sweep's file states every mechanical step of its batched call. It also keeps following answer-with-recommendation-procedure.md, but only for the lift step's definitions: ANSWER is the lift's whole printed line, RECORDED OPTION is the text before the first spaced em dash, and both come from that print alone, never from an applied-principle or alternative (the provenance-free derivation). Like "Core judgment only", it follows answer-procedure.md for the analyse step and the fold-content rules. Both procedures' intros are reworded to say which of their parts the sweep follows. The CLAUDE.md wording "The lift lives in that procedure" stays true for the sweep as well. The derivation rule that keeps a recorded decision provenance-free stays in one file for both recommendation-recording paths, so the sweep and answer-open-question-with-recommendation cannot drift on what a lifted line yields. The sweep would reference a one-paragraph definition from a procedure whose other two parts (the stop-and-report guard and the wholesale delegation to the core) it overrides, so two procedures need step-level partial-follower wording instead of one. How the batched call gets its remove option value depends on the option-value-source question and may make the RECORDED OPTION definition moot for the sweep.

The sweep's own file states every per-question step: the mechanics of the batched call (lift and its silent skip, the fold through the fold command, remove with the lifted option, the commit, the stop after a fold) and whatever per-question judgment the sweep keeps. That includes the fold-content rules (clean prose, no citation marker, the live document's section names) and the ANSWER and option derivation from the lift's print. It follows neither answer procedure. Both procedures' intros say they are followed by the single-question skills alone, with no other change to their text. The CLAUDE.md sweep invariant drops "following answer-with-recommendation-procedure.md from its lift step", and the shell-literal clause drops its "per-question calls of the procedures it follows" wording. The sweep's file is a complete account of what a run does, with no cross-file exception list. The shared procedures go back to describing one question recorded by hand-paced steps, with no batched reader to keep in mind, which matches the goal's split that only the sweep uses the fold command. The rules for decision text and option derivation now exist in two places, answer-procedure.md for the three single-question skills and the sweep's file for the sweep. A later change to how a decision is worded or where it lands has to be made twice or the paths drift. How much judgment the sweep's file has to restate depends on the mooting-cascade and contradiction-advisory questions.

open-question.question: The compact view gives the sweep each walked question's id, question text, and lifted pick, that is the option id and the recommendation's one-line rationale, and the whole XML is no longer read, while today's folds draw the recorded decision's detail from the picked alternative's what-it-is text. Is each sweep decision written from the lifted line alone, or does the compact view also carry the picked alternative's what-it-is text for every walked id?
open-question.alternative: The compact view stays exactly as decided: list --with-question, then each walked id with its lift line. Nothing else about the question document is fetched. Each sweep decision is written from the block's question text, the option id, and the recommendation's one-line rationale alone, at the detail those carry. No lift --alternative, locate, or other read of the picked alternative happens at any point in the run. The view, its one fixed call, and the setup turn count stay exactly as the Compact view command decision fixed them, with no extra value, parse, or call. The decision is drawn only from the line that also becomes the commit body, so the recorded text and the commit record say the same thing. The option id is a short label and the rationale states reasons rather than positions. The concrete content of the pick, which today's folds take from the what-it-is (the stop-report decision's silenced lift stderr and fixed stopped-at line, for instance), is either left out or rebuilt by the runner from the label and the question text, which is the invented answer text the lift procedure forbids. Sweep decisions then carry less than the hand-answer skills' decisions, which keep their locate, while `## Decisions` is what derive-tasks and later reviews read.

The compact view's fixed call is extended, still one call with no tool change. Inside its walk-fed loop, after printing each id and its lift line, it takes the option id from that line in the shell (the text before the first spaced em dash, by parameter expansion on the held line), runs lift --alternative with it, and prints that alternative's what-it-is line beneath. A walked id whose lift fails prints its Error: line and no alternative line. Every walked id with a pick gets its what-it-is, and each decision is written from the question text, the lifted line, and that what-it-is. The remove --option value is still the runner's literal copy of the option. Every sweep decision keeps the detail today's folds draw from the located block, the concrete positions that the option id and the rationale's reasons leave out. It costs no extra turn and needs no judgment about which picks need it. The view still leaves out the unpicked alternatives and every advantage and drawback, so it stays far smaller than the XML. The fixed call gains a second per-item shell value and a shell-side split of the lifted line. That is the same first-spaced-em-dash split the lift procedure defines for RECORDED OPTION, now done in the shell and used only for display, and the shell-literal clause for the sweep must cover the extra value too. The view also grows by one what-it-is per walked block, text with no length limit, which narrows the measured 9–13× saving over the XML. Whether this added shell logic is caught by anything besides the hands-on check depends on the axis the Compact view test coverage question owns.

The compact view's call stays exactly as decided. After reading its print, the runner composes and runs a second call. It holds one lift --alternative per walked id whose lift succeeded, each with the block's Short Title and the option id copied literally from the compact view's lift line, and each invocation written as the full fixed command. The runner reads its print before composing the batched call. Every walked pick gets its what-it-is, and each decision is written from the question text, the lifted line, and that what-it-is. Every decision gets the full detail while the compact view's fixed call and its decided shape stay untouched. The option reaches lift --alternative as an exact id the runner copied, the same discipline the batched call keeps for remove --option, with no shell-side parse of the answer text. Every run that walks a pick pays one more setup turn, which must come after the compact view because the ids come from its print. That works against the goal of collapsing the setup to its fixed-call floor. The second call is composed per run rather than fixed and run as shown, so it is one more runner-written template beside the batched call, and the context grows by the same what-it-is text as carrying it in the view.

The compact view's call stays exactly as decided, and each decision is written from the question text and the lifted line by default. When the runner judges that a pick's question text, option id, and rationale do not state concretely enough what was decided, it fetches the what-it-is of those picks only. It does so before composing the batched call, in one call of lift --alternative lines with the option ids copied literally. A run whose lifted lines all suffice fetches nothing. A run pays for the alternative text only where the lifted line falls short. Runs whose rationales already name the decided positions keep the decided view and turn count, and thin picks still get their detail. It adds a per-pick judgment to a sweep otherwise made a pure recorder of picks as given, and the setup no longer has a fixed call count. A miss is silent: a thin decision is folded and committed with nothing flagging it. Option ids are short labels and the rationale is written as brief reasons, so many picks are likely to need the fetch, and the option then tends to cost what the separate call costs plus the judgment.

The compact view stays as decided, and each decision is written from the question text and the lifted line alone, with no what-it-is fetched by the sweep. In addition, the recommendation pass's rendering and recommend-procedure.md are changed so that the one-line rationale states the picked option's concrete positions as well as why it was picked. That makes the lifted line enough for the fold on its own. The sweep's view and calls stay minimal, with no parse and no extra turn. The one line the sweep reads, which is also the commit body that capture walks, carries the decision's substance, so the commit body alone tells what was decided. It widens the milestone to the recommendation pass and its procedure, which the goal does not name. Picks already standing, in this milestone and in other projects, were formed under the brief-rationale rule and stay thin until they are re-picked. The rationale stops being a brief reason and restates the what-it-is in a second place, which lengthens every pick and every Recommendation-answer body that capture reads as evidence.

open-question.question: The goal keeps the whole read of requirements.md beside the compact view, but the compact view's fixed call covers the question document only. Is requirements.md read with the file-reading tool as a separate step, as today, or is that read written into the same fixed shell call so the sweep's setup is one call?
open-question.alternative: requirements.md is read whole with the file-reading tool as its own setup step, in its own turn after the compact view's fixed call, as today; the compact view call stays limited to the question document, and the skill shows no shell command for the read. It changes nothing beyond what the compact view decision already fixes. The read stays on the file-reading tool, so no shell output cap and no shell parsing can affect it, and the wording reads the same in all three host trees with no slot. Setup stays one turn above its floor. Once the batched call shrinks the loop to about one turn, this extra turn, at about 45k tokens of context in the field measurement, is one of only a few turns in the run, and the sweep's setup is not one call.

requirements.md is read whole with the file-reading tool, and the skill tells the runner to send that read in the same turn as the compact view's fixed shell call, as two independent tool calls. The file never goes through shell output, and the compact view call stays limited to the question document. It reaches the setup floor on Claude Code, where 15 of 88 measured runs already paired their reads with walk this way unprompted, while the whole read stays on the file-reading tool. No shell output cap applies, and the compact view call keeps the shape its decision describes. It is an instruction about sending tool calls in parallel, and the sweep's identical, slot-free text would state it for all three hosts while only Claude Code is hands-on checked. On a host that sends one call per turn the sentence is dead text, the capability-conditional prose the slot invariant avoids, unless the sweep gains its first wording slot.

The compact view's fixed shell call also prints requirements.md with a literal cat of <MILESTONE_DIR>/requirements.md, behind one fixed header line printed with printf that does not begin with =. Setup becomes one shell call, shown in full and run as shown with only <MILESTONE_DIR> replaced, and the file-reading tool is not used for this read. Setup is one call and one turn on every host using plain shell, and because the separator is fixed in the shown command, the echo ===== line that failed in zsh in 33 of 88 runs cannot be written back in. The setup follows the same fixed-call pattern as the rest of the rewritten sweep. The whole read now travels as shell output. Claude Code 2.1.302 passes only 30,000 characters of a Bash result inline and saves the rest to a file behind a preview, and this repository's recent requirements.md files run 14k to 31k characters at finish, before the compact view's own print is added. On a large milestone the print spills and costs the read-back turn it was meant to save, and the other hosts' output caps are unchecked.

open-question.question: A stop after a fold leaves a decision folded into requirements.md but uncommitted, and the sweep is re-run from the top after a fix, with no clean-tree precondition today. Does the batched sweep check that its two files are clean before recording anything and stop on a dirty one, or does it run regardless, letting a stranded fold ride into the first answer's commit?
open-question.alternative: No check of the milestone's open_questions.xml and requirements.md at any point, never rather than deferred: the sweep keeps today's lack of a clean-tree precondition, the batched call starts its first question's section whatever the two files hold, and a stop after a fold leaves the tree exactly as it stands, never rolled back. A stranded fold, or a fold plus block removal left by a refused commit, rides into the first Recommendation-answer: commit the re-run lands. The stop report can name the remedy (discard the uncommitted fold with a checkout, as the Fold refusal set decision describes, or commit a hand fix), but nothing in the run checks for or clears the leftover. The batched call and the setup keep their decided shape, with no guard line, no new stop branch, and no new report wording, and the case is rare: the field measurement found one failed remove in 856 answers, and the resume the Fold refusal set decision already relies on is a single checkout the stop report can point to. A stop nobody acts on corrupts the record without any sign. After a refused remove the re-run folds the stopped question again, so its decision appears twice in requirements.md. After a refused commit, the stopped question's fold and block removal ride into the next question's commit under that question's subject, so capture reconstructs two answered blocks from one commit and reverting it reopens both. A headless chain, where nobody reads the stop report, is the likeliest place for this.

The batched call's first command, ahead of the first question's section, runs git status --porcelain on the milestone's open_questions.xml and requirements.md, each path written as its own literal argument. When that prints anything, the call prints one fixed line with no identifier (for example "uncommitted changes carried") and goes on into the sections without stopping. The report step then adds one advisory beside the status line: the first landed commit also carries changes made before the run. A stop after a fold still leaves the tree as it stands, never rolled back. A re-run never stops on leftovers, so a headless chain resumed after a fix keeps going. The run's own output names the contamination the first commit absorbs, which git alone never shows, since a commit diff does not say which part was there before the run. It reports the damage instead of preventing it. The duplicate fold or the misattributed block removal still lands in history, and undoing it still takes reverting and re-answering two questions. It also adds an advisory that the terse-reporting rule must accept as both git-absent and decision-critical.

A clean-own-paths precondition in the batched call. Its first command, ahead of the first question's section, runs git status --porcelain on the milestone's open_questions.xml and requirements.md, each path its own literal argument. If that prints anything, the call prints one fixed line (for example "dirty before start") and ends before any lift, fold, remove, or commit. Any staged or unstaged change counts, whatever its origin. The report step prints this stop with the porcelain lines and the remedy (commit or discard the leftover, then re-run) in place of the status line. A stop after a fold still leaves the tree as it stands, never rolled back. The skill's sentence saying it needs no clean working tree narrows to these two files only, never the whole tree. No commit can carry a change made before the run, so one-commit-per-answer and capture's per-commit reconstruction stay true across re-runs. The guard sits inside the one fixed template, where the decided template test can add a dirty-start case next to its other assertions, and the compact view call stays exactly as decided. It stops on every leftover, including the hand fix to requirements.md that the Fold refusal handling decision expects before a re-run, so a fix left uncommitted blocks the re-run until someone commits it by hand. The stop also fires only after the runner has read requirements.md and composed the whole batched call, the run's most expensive turn.

The same clean-own-paths precondition, run before the sweep reads anything instead of inside the batched call. It is git status --porcelain on the milestone's open_questions.xml and requirements.md, each path its own literal argument, and any staged or unstaged change stops the run with the porcelain lines and the commit-or-discard remedy. It runs either as the first command of the compact view call, ahead of its list, or as its own call before that one. The batched call carries no guard, and a stop after a fold still leaves the tree as it stands, never rolled back. A dirty tree stops the run before it reads requirements.md or composes the batched call, so the rare stop costs one call instead of a full compose turn, and the runner never reasons over a requirements.md that holds a stranded fold. It either amends the decided compact view call, which runs list and then the walk-fed lift loop and nothing else, or adds a setup turn against the goal's fixed-call floor. The guard sits outside the batched template, so whether any test pins it depends on whether the compact view call is tested, an axis the Compact view test coverage question owns. Like any guard, it also stops on an uncommitted hand fix to requirements.md.

No stop at start. Before the sweep reads anything, its first setup command runs git status --porcelain on the milestone's open_questions.xml and requirements.md. When that prints anything, it restores both files to their committed state with git checkout HEAD -- and the two literal paths, prints one fixed line saying leftovers were discarded, and continues against the restored files. A stop after a fold still leaves the tree as it stands, for the next run's restore to clear. A re-run after a stop resumes with no human step. The stranded fold and any block removal are discarded before the compact view is built, so the stopped question is walked again, folded once, and committed under its own subject. This suits the headless chains, where nobody is there to clean up. It destroys every uncommitted change to the two files without asking, including the hand fix the Fold refusal handling decision expects. A fold refusal fixed by hand but not committed therefore refuses again on every re-run, and a user's in-progress edit to requirements.md is lost. The restore also writes open_questions.xml outside the open-question tool, which the sweep's stop rule forbids today. It puts a destructive git command in every run's setup, which prompts in an interactive session and runs unseen in a headless chain.

This rejects the premise that a stop strands the fold. There is no check at start. Instead, in every question's section, the failure branch of each step after the fold (the remove or the commit) restores the milestone's open_questions.xml and requirements.md to HEAD, index included, with git checkout HEAD -- and the two literal paths, before it prints its stop line. A stop therefore leaves the two files at the last landed answer's commit. This reverses the sweep's never-rolled-back stop rule and the CLAUDE.md invariant that states it. It removes the case at its source with no precondition and no new stop branch. Every tool or commit failure leaves the two files clean, so a plain re-run after the fix resumes correctly, and a hand fix made after a fold refusal never blocks the re-run. It does not cover a call ended mid-section by an interrupt or a killed shell, which still strands a fold that the next run carries into its first commit. Without a start check, changes made before the run ride into the first commit, or are discarded if the first section fails. It reverses a recorded invariant, loses the failed section's partial state as evidence, and writes open_questions.xml outside the open-question tool.

Both mechanisms, both in the batched call. Its first command is the clean-own-paths precondition: git status --porcelain on the milestone's open_questions.xml and requirements.md, each path its own literal argument, and any staged or unstaged change ends the call with a fixed line and the commit-or-discard remedy. In addition, the failure branch of every step after a fold restores both files to HEAD, index included, before printing its stop line. This reverses the sweep's never-rolled-back stop rule and its CLAUDE.md invariant. Each mechanism covers what the other misses. The guard proves the two files matched HEAD when the call started, and every earlier section committed, so the restore returns exactly the state before the section and loses nothing. Every tool or commit failure then resumes with a plain re-run, while leftovers from an interrupted call or a hand edit are stopped instead of committed. It is the largest change to the template and the skill: a guard, a restore in every section, and a reversed recorded invariant together. It puts a destructive git command in every section's failure branch and writes open_questions.xml outside the open-question tool. The guard still blocks a re-run on an uncommitted hand fix after a fold refusal.

open-question.question: When the review pass's new Decisions consistency step finds two recorded decisions in conflict, does it author an open-question block asking which entry stands, committed with the pass like any other new gap, or only flag the pair in the pass's report beside the still-open list?
open-question.alternative: The consistency step authors one block per conflicting pair through the open-question tool's `add`, its question text naming both entries' `###` headings under `## Decisions` and asking which entry stands, and the block is committed in the pass's `Requirements-review:` commit like any other new gap. The report gains no new advisory: the block shows only as a Short Title in the still-open list, and the convergence verdict is still read from the `list` print alone, so the conflict holds convergence and the `derive-tasks` precondition until the block is answered. The block then goes through the alternatives pass, the recommendation pass, and either the sweep or a hand answer like any other question. The conflict becomes committed state that outlives the run and that the existing precondition enforces: `derive-tasks` cannot run past it, in a headless chain included. It is resolved through the answer skills, so the settling choice lands as an answer commit with a provenance marker that capture reads. It is the form the recorded Contradiction detection decision gives as its example, and it needs no new report advisory, no change to the convergence rule, and no tool change. Answering can only add. The answer core's fold and the sweep's verbatim fold append a settling entry and neither removes nor rewords the losing one, so `## Decisions` ends up holding the conflicting pair plus a third entry saying which stands, and the next consistency step must read that entry as covering the pair or it raises the same conflict again. In the chains of `docs/ways-of-using-cairn.md` the recommendation pass picks which recorded decision stands and the sweep records it with no person in the loop.

The consistency step authors no block and commits nothing for the conflict. It prints each conflicting pair, as the two entries' `###` headings, as one advisory beside the still-open list in the step-5 report, a git-absent decision-critical advisory under the terse-report rule. The convergence verdict is unchanged and still read from the `list` print alone, so a converged question document is still reported ready for `derive-tasks` with the pair listed beside it. The conflict is resolved by hand-editing `## Decisions`, and every pass re-detects it until then. The question document keeps holding only questions about gaps in the requirements, so no choice between two already-recorded decisions goes through the annotating passes to be recorded by a sweep without a person. Whoever resolves it can delete or reword the losing entry directly, leaving a clean `## Decisions` that the add-only answer fold cannot produce, and the convergence verdict and the `derive-tasks` precondition stay one test. The flag is transient and stops nothing. In a headless chain no one reads the review's report, and the stuck-milestone chain in `docs/ways-of-using-cairn.md` runs `derive-tasks` after its review with no stop, so a conflict reaches task derivation. This is the same report-only shape this milestone retires from the sweep. The hand edit that resolves it goes through no skill and carries no answer marker, and the pair is printed again every pass with no record that it was seen.

The consistency step authors no block and commits nothing for the conflict. It prints each conflicting pair, as the two entries' `###` headings, as an advisory beside the still-open list, as in the report-only form, but the convergence verdict also reads that flag: while any pair is flagged the report says the requirements are not ready, even when `list` printed nothing. The `derive-tasks` precondition stays an empty question document. The conflict is resolved by hand-editing `## Decisions`, after which the next pass finds no pair and can report convergence. Someone running the review loop by hand and watching the verdict is told not to move on past a known conflict, and the conflict still stays out of the question flow, where the annotating passes and a sweep would settle it automatically. The hand edit that resolves it can still remove the losing entry outright. The verdict stops meaning an empty question document, so it and the `derive-tasks` precondition diverge: `derive-tasks` still runs past the flag, and the headless chains, which never read the verdict, gain nothing over the report-only form. No skill clears the flag, so the loop cannot converge until someone edits `## Decisions` by hand, and the review skill's convergence rule and its documentation have to change with it.

open-question.question: The batched-call test extracts the fixed call from a rendered sweep file and fills its per-question placeholders, but nothing yet says how the test finds the call and its repeating per-question section. By what anchor in the rendered file does the test locate them, so the skill's author and the test share one shape every later edit must keep?
open-question.alternative: The test finds the call as the one fenced block of the rendered sweep file that holds a command only the call carries (the fold command), and fails when no fence or more than one fence holds it. It finds the per-question section by lines the call already needs: from the section's fixed opening line through the column-0 line that closes it, the same span the step's prose names to the runner as the lines written once per question. Everything from the fixed header line printed before the completeness walk to the end of the fence is the footer, written once. Nothing is added to the runtime file for the test. The test keys on the shape the runner already needs, stated once in the runner-facing sentence that says which lines repeat (the recommendation pass names its section the same way, "the lines from if { through the fi that closes it"). No test-only text enters a runtime file, and the author and the test read one boundary. Nothing in the file marks those lines as something a test depends on. An edit that adds a column-0 if or fi inside the section, rewords its opening line, or moves the walk header breaks extraction, and the editor learns the anchor only from a failing CI run or the test's docstring.

The test finds the call as the fenced block under the step heading that holds the batched call, matched on the heading's title text. It finds the per-question section and the footer by the call's own fixed lines, as in the call's-own-lines option: the section runs from its opening line through the line that closes it, and the footer starts at the walk header line. Finding the fence does not depend on what the call contains, so a later edit that renames a command, reorders the chain, or changes how the fold tool is invoked never loses the fence. Only the lines that bound the section have to hold. Ties the test to the skill's step structure, which milestones edit routinely (this milestone itself collapses the sweep's setup steps). Retitling or splitting the step, or adding a second fence under it, breaks the test through an edit that never touched the call.

A fixed marker outside the shell text identifies the call: an HTML comment line directly above its fence, or a distinctive fence info string. The test finds the fence by that marker alone, and finds the per-question section and the footer by the call's own fixed lines, as in the call's-own-lines option. The fence is found whatever is edited around it or inside it, and the marker tells a later editor that a test depends on the fence, all without adding a character to the text the runner copies and runs. It puts test-facing text into a runtime file, against the invariant that runtime files hold only what the runner needs, and in a form no core file uses today (core holds no HTML comment, and its only info strings are markdown, md, and bash). The section boundary inside the fence stays as implicit as it would be with no marker.

Two fixed shell comment lines inside the fenced call bracket the per-question section, one directly before it and one directly after it. The test finds the call as the fence that holds them, takes the lines between them as the section, and takes the lines after the closing one as the footer. The step's prose tells the runner to repeat what lies between them. It gives the most explicit boundary. Extraction keeps working through any rewrite of the section's shell (a nested if, a reordered chain, a reworded opening line) as long as the two lines stay, and both the runner and the editor see exactly what repeats and that a test depends on it. It adds lines to the text the runner copies into the call it runs. None of the plugin's fixed calls carries such lines yet, so no hands-on check covers how each host's shell parses them, and the call's executable text now carries structure that exists for the test.

The step shows the call as two fences instead of one. The first holds the per-question section alone, written once per question, and the second holds the footer (the header line and the completeness walk), written once after the last section. The test finds the section fence as the one holding the fold command and the footer fence as the one holding the walk header, so the fence boundary is the section boundary and no line inside either fence serves as an anchor. The boundary is Markdown structure that no edit of the shell text can blur, so the test needs no shell-aware matching and the section's contents can change freely. It departs from the single fence in which every batched-call precedent shows its whole call. The runner has to assemble one call from two shown blocks, and a runner that runs each fence as shown would run a section or the footer on its own.

No section boundary is part of the shape. The test finds the call as the one fence holding the fold command, fills every per-question placeholder in the whole fence for a single fixture question, and runs the filled call once per question, so the call's only anchors are that fence and its placeholder tokens. A later edit only has to keep one fence and the placeholder tokens, so the section can be restructured, nested, or reworded with no change to the test. The test never runs two sections in one call. It cannot show that a skipped lift lets the next question's section run, that copied sections compose (heredoc delimiters, one marker per landed commit, the walk header after many sections), or that the footer runs once. The decided skip assertion shrinks to "no commit for that question", and the walk runs once per question.

This milestone's requirements decide no anchor. The task that writes the test chooses one against the batched call as the rewritten skill actually shows it and records it in the test module's docstring. The skill's rewrite carries no rule about it. The anchor is fitted to the call as written rather than to a template that does not exist yet, and the requirements carry no implementation detail that the rewrite could make wrong. The skill's rewrite and the test may land as separate tasks completed by separate agents, so neither agrees in advance on the shape the two must share, which is exactly the gap the question names. A later editor of the skill finds the anchor only in the test or through a CI failure.
